title: DOJ Office of Legal Counsel Opinion Rejects ADA/Rehabilitation Act Integration Mandate for State Institutionalization
description_short: DOJ Office of Legal Counsel Opinion Rejects ADA/Rehabilitation Act Integration Mandate for State Institutionalization
description_medium: On June 18, 2026, the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel issued an opinion rejecting a federal integration mandate under the ADA and Rehabilitation Act for state treatment of people with mental disabilities. The opinion disputed the prevailing reading of Olmstead v. L.C.; Senator Tammy Duckworth and colleagues introduced a resolution urging DOJ to rescind it.
description_long: The Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel issued its opinion on June 18, 2026. It concluded that Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act do not require states to provide services in the most integrated setting for people with mental disabilities, and do not authorize federal agencies to impose that requirement. The opinion also said the Supreme Court’s 1999 decision in Olmstead v. L.C. did not establish such a mandate, while acknowledging that its interpretation differs from the common understanding of Olmstead in federal courts. On June 25, Senator Tammy Duckworth, joined by Senators Chuck Schumer and Dick Durbin, introduced a resolution calling on the Justice Department to rescind the opinion and reaffirm the protections associated with Olmstead. The dispute concerns whether federal disability statutes require states to prioritize community-based treatment over institutional care and how far federal agencies may go in enforcing that principle. The opinion changes DOJ’s stated legal position; the senators’ resolution challenges that interpretation.

title: LGBTQ Asylum Seekers Abandoned: Refugee Cap Slashed 94 Percent, White Afrikaners Prioritized
description_short: LGBTQ Asylum Seekers Abandoned: Refugee Cap Slashed 94 Percent, White Afrikaners Prioritized
description_medium: The FY 2026 refugee determination set a U.S. admissions ceiling of 7,500 and said the places would be allocated primarily to Afrikaners from South Africa and other people facing discrimination in their home countries. The cap was 94 percent below the Biden administration’s 125,000-person target, sharply narrowing the program after Trump had suspended refugee admissions.
description_long: The presidential determination for fiscal year 2026 allowed up to 7,500 refugees to be admitted to the United States, compared with the Biden administration’s 125,000-person target. It said admissions should be allocated primarily to Afrikaners from South Africa, along with other people facing illegal or unjust discrimination in their home countries. That allocation made the South African group the chief priority within a sharply reduced national ceiling. The policy followed Trump’s January 20, 2025 suspension of the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program, which left 128,000 already vetted refugees waiting, including people fleeing persecution based on sexual orientation or gender identity. A Williams Institute analysis described how the cap could exclude LGBTQ refugees who often lack family-reunification pathways. Immigration Equality also documented an encounter in which an ICE officer allegedly restrained an LGBTQ asylum seeker and threatened her wife with self-deportation. The lower ceiling narrowed resettlement capacity while prioritizing Afrikaners and other named groups.

title: Donald Trump Announces 2024 Presidential Campaign at Mar-a-Lago Under Cloud of Federal and State Probes
description_short: Donald Trump Announces 2024 Presidential Campaign at Mar-a-Lago Under Cloud of Federal and State Probes
description_medium: Donald Trump announced his 2024 presidential campaign at Mar-a-Lago on November 15, 2022, one week after midterm results disappointed many candidates he had endorsed. He made the announcement while facing active criminal and civil investigations, then pledged to reclaim the White House and repeated claims about his record.
description_long: Donald Trump announced that he would run for president again in 2024 during a speech at his Mar-a-Lago estate on November 15, 2022. The announcement came one week after midterm results disappointed candidates he had endorsed and while he faced multiple criminal and civil investigations. Trump pledged to reclaim the White House and repeated claims about his presidential record. Political analysts described the early launch as a way to establish a public political response to possible Justice Department indictments. The launch put his political comeback on the calendar while federal and state investigations continued.

title: Gag Order Battles in Trump NY Hush Money Case
description_short: Gag Order Battles in Trump NY Hush Money Case
description_medium: Throughout 2023 in the Manhattan hush money case, Judge Juan Merchan issued a limited gag order preventing Trump from attacking witnesses and family members of court officials. Trump repeatedly tested the order boundaries by posting attacks on Michael Cohen and other potential witnesses on Truth Social. The ongoing tension between Trump free speech claims and witness protection became a defining feature of the case. Merchan warned Trump faced consequences for violations including possible jail.
description_long: On May 8, 2023, Judge Juan Merchan entered a protective order limiting how the defense could share evidence from prosecutors in Donald Trump’s Manhattan hush-money case. The order confined discovery materials to preparing the defense and barred people with access from copying or disclosing them without court approval. Trump could review sensitive materials only with his lawyers present and could not independently copy or keep them. The order separately restricted access to forensic images of witnesses’ phones, though lawyers could show him approved portions after getting permission. Prosecutors said they sought safeguards for evidence rather than a general gag order; Trump’s lawyers argued the proposed limits would infringe his and the public’s First Amendment rights.

title: Maine Secretary of State Removes Trump from Ballot
description_short: Maine Secretary of State Removes Trump from Ballot
description_medium: On December 28, 2023, Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows became the first state official to unilaterally remove a presidential candidate from the ballot, ruling Trump disqualified under the 14th Amendment insurrection clause. Bellows cited Trump role in the January 6 Capitol attack in her decision. Trump appealed. The ruling was stayed pending Supreme Court review. Combined with the Colorado ruling, the decisions forced the Supreme Court to definitively address whether January 6 constituted insurrection.
description_long: On December 28, 2023, Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows ruled that Donald Trump was disqualified from the state’s presidential ballot under Section 3 of the Fourteenth Amendment, citing his conduct around the January 6 Capitol attack. Trump appealed, and the decision was stayed while courts reviewed the dispute. The decision joined a similar Colorado challenge in a national debate over whether Section 3 bars a presidential candidate and how states can apply it. The Supreme Court later considered related ballot-access questions.
organization_tags: Supreme Court of the United States

title: Trump Hotels & Casino Resorts Third Bankruptcy Filing
description_short: Trump Hotels & Casino Resorts Third Bankruptcy Filing
description_medium: UPI reported that Trump Castle and Trump Plaza filed prepackaged Chapter 11 plans in March 1992 after bondholders approved debt restructurings. The plans followed the Taj Mahal’s bankruptcy reorganization and responded to heavy casino debt and falling revenue. Castle’s deal exchanged bonds for equity while Trump retained management fees.
description_long: On March 9, 1992, UPI reported that Trump Castle and Trump Plaza had filed prepackaged Chapter 11 plans after bondholders approved restructurings intended to reduce interest costs. The filings followed the Trump Taj Mahal’s reorganization the previous year. Holders of 77 percent of Castle’s debt and 97 percent of Plaza’s debt approved their respective plans. Under Castle’s arrangement, the Trump Organization gave up a 50 percent share of the casino’s stock to bondholders, who exchanged higher-interest debt for lower-rate bonds; some interest could be paid in additional bonds rather than cash. Plaza bondholders agreed to exchange $250 million in bonds for $225 million in bonds and $75 million in preferred stock. Both casinos had heavy debt loads, and revenues had fallen since the Taj Mahal opened in April 1990 amid weak Atlantic City revenues, recession, and the Persian Gulf War. The plans retained Trump management fees but allowed bondholders to remove him if financial problems continued. The plans reduced interest expenses but exchanged a substantial equity stake and stock for debt relief, while allowing bondholders to remove Trump if the financial problems continued.
organization_tags: U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of New Jersey

title: Trump Model Management Recruits Models on Improper Visas
description_short: Trump Model Management Recruits Models on Improper Visas
description_medium: A 2016 Mother Jones investigation reported that former models at Trump Model Management worked commercially in the United States on tourist visas that did not authorize employment. Three models described their experiences; records in a fourth model’s lawsuit also showed work without proper authorization. Models said housing and agency fees left some in debt.
description_long: Mother Jones reported in 2016 that three former noncitizen models said Trump Model Management brought them to the United States on tourist visas that did not permit them to work. Financial and immigration records filed in a fourth former model’s lawsuit also showed work for the agency without proper authorization. The article explains that tourist visas generally bar employment and that employers can face fines or criminal charges for using undocumented labor. Former models described agency-arranged housing and charges for rent and other expenses. One model said her bookings did not cover her living costs and that she left New York indebted to the agency. A former model quoted in the investigation characterized the arrangement as a system that made money from foreign workers through fees. The reporting connected the workers’ accounts to broader modeling-industry allegations about agencies charging excessive housing costs.

title: RFK Jr Nominated to HHS
description_medium: Trump nominated Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to lead the Department of Health and Human Services. RFK Jr. is a prominent anti-vaccine conspiracy theorist who has spread disinformation about health and science for decades. Medical professionals expressed deep alarm that a science denier would be in charge of the nation's premier health agencies, including the CDC, FDA, and NIH.
description_long: Donald Trump nominated Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to lead the Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees agencies including the CDC, FDA, and NIH. Kennedy had spent years promoting claims that vaccines are unsafe and disputing established health and science findings. Medical professionals expressed alarm at the prospect of his leading the country’s main public-health agencies. The nomination put a longtime vaccine critic in line to oversee federal research, disease response, and medicine regulation.

title: DOGE Leadership and Musk-Company Regulatory Oversight in Early 2025
description_short: DOGE Leadership and Musk-Company Regulatory Oversight in Early 2025
description_medium: Elon Musk led the Department of Government Efficiency while Tesla remained under federal safety oversight. In October 2025, NHTSA opened a new preliminary evaluation into reports of traffic-safety violations involving Tesla’s Full Self-Driving system. The agency had also said an earlier FSD probe would continue, showing the investigation remained active during Musk’s government role.
description_long: Elon Musk led the Department of Government Efficiency while his companies, including Tesla, remained subject to federal regulation. In January 2025, Reuters reported that transportation secretary nominee Sean Duffy said an existing Tesla Full Self-Driving safety probe would continue. In October, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened Preliminary Evaluation PE25012 to examine reports that Tesla vehicles using Full Self-Driving violated traffic-safety laws. The evaluation was preliminary: NHTSA opened a fact-finding step but had not announced a final safety finding or recall. Its opening followed Duffy’s assurance by about nine months and showed continued federal scrutiny of the driver-assistance system during Musk’s government role. The overlapping responsibilities raised ethics questions about independent oversight of a senior official’s private companies. The overlap placed Tesla’s federal safety oversight and Musk’s government role in the same ethics debate, without evidence that Musk directed this investigation.
